transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-05
Start time (host TZ): 11:00 PT / 14:00 ET
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Liam Torres (Enso CTO), Priya Singh (Enso Infra Lead), Alex Gomez (Enso ML Eng)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood — Ravi is our solutions engineer — we'll run you through a short edge-cases demo focused on long context and high TPS streaming patterns. Quick note, I'll share the deck and benchmarks afterward.

[00:18] Liam Torres: Great, thanks — we only got 60 minutes so appreciate it. Our main interest is how you handle really long contexts, we have logs + telemetry that can be >50k tokens in some cases, plus bursts during fleet updates where TPS spikes.

[00:33] Maya Chen: Perfect — we'll show console + API flows. Ravi, do you want to kick off with the long-context behavior?

[00:40] Ravi Patel: Yeah, sure. So first thing — Redwood supports long context modes, we surface model variants and tokenization strategies in the Console. In practice for >32k tokens we do a couple things: chunking with smart prefix retention, a KV cache to store reusable attention state, and fallbacks to quantized variants when memory is constrained.

[01:05] Alex Gomez: Quick question — when you say KV cache, is that per-session or global? How do you evict?

[01:12] Ravi Patel: Good question — KV cache is per model instance and per session, so it's sticky to a conversation. Eviction is LRU-ish plus TTL; we also expose metrics so you can tune eviction and prewarming behavior. One caveat — occasionally transcriptions call it K V cash or K V catch, so docs have both spelled out.

[01:32] Priya Singh: If we have multi-tenant VPC deployment, does the cache live in customer VM/GPU memory or in a separate cache tier?

[01:40] Ravi Patel: For Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) the KV cache stays on the serving host memory/GPU to minimize token latency. For hosted, it's colocated with the runtime in our tenant-isolated infra. If you want persistence we can persist keys to a local fast store but then you trade off cold-start latency.

[01:58] Liam Torres: And how do you handle sequence length discontinuities? e.g., we may prepend 40k tokens but only need last 8k for generation — do you trim?

[02:08] Ravi Patel: We do heuristics: prefix compression, selective retention based on recency/salience, and a user-configurable window. If you need deterministic behavior we can pin clip-length and fall back to summarization pipeline before the model.

[02:25] Maya Chen: I'll quickly share my screen to show the Console where you can adjust those settings and view per-route token distribution.

[02:40] [screen share starts]

[02:45] Ravi Patel: On the Console you can see a route for long-context-chat-prod. On the right panel there's a 'Context policy' dropdown: keep-last-n, KV-augmented, or summarize+chop. You also get a histogram of token counts by request so you can spot the 40k spikes.

[03:10] Alex Gomez: That histogram's nice. For our use case we want deterministic fallbacks; can we route to a smaller model when context > threshold?

[03:18] Ravi Patel: Yes — routing policies let you map by token-length to model variants and capacity tiers. So you can route normal flows to high-quality LLM and overflow to a cheaper/run faster quantized variant. It also plays with cost controls so you don't get bill shock during bursts.

[03:34] Priya Singh: OK, let's talk high TPS — we can see bursts up to 1k TPS for short periods during fleet sync events. How does Redwood handle backpressure and streaming timeouts?

[03:44] Ravi Patel: High TPS, especially with streaming, is where the runtime's batching and streaming backpressure logic matters. We do continuous batching with a token-aware scheduler. For streaming we support partial-chunk flushes and explicit backpressure signals in the SDKs. If a client can't keep up we'll buffer to a configurable soft limit, then apply two policies: slow-client drop (fastfail) or slow-client stall (block) depending on your SLOs.

[04:12] Liam Torres: How often do you hit timeouts with stall behavior? Our infra does strict 30s client timeouts.

[04:18] Ravi Patel: It depends — if you have many long contexts the per-token latency can increase. We recommend an upper bound on request wall-time and a streaming heartbeat so the client knows activity continues. For strict 30s client timeouts we usually implement an ack-first pattern: send an immediate small metadata chunk then stream the rest. Also you can set per-route server-side timeouts in Console — then falling back to a smaller model or a precomputed cached response avoids client-visible timeout.

[04:45] Alex Gomez: Could you demo a streaming scenario where clients apply backpressure?

[04:50] Ravi Patel: Yep — I'll run a simulated load. Note: the demo infra here is limited but should be representative.

[05:00] [demo: simulated TPS ramp on console, log window open]

[05:10] Ravi Patel: Starting a burst — ramping to ~800 TPS for 30s. Watch the stream window: you'll see some partial chunks delivered, then a small spike in server-side queue depth.

[05:28] [console logs]

[05:30] Liam Torres: I see a few stalled streams with "client-slow" metrics — do you surface those as alerts?

[05:36] Ravi Patel: Yes, we surface client-slow, queue-depth, avg-per-token latency per route and per model. You can wire those to alerts in Console. For this demo we're on hosted — with Dedicated you'd get reserved capacity so the queue depth stays lower.

[05:50] Priya Singh: For Dedicated, do you have SLA numbers for tail latency during bursts?

[05:55] Ravi Patel: SLA is configurable per plan, but typical committed latency SLOs are 95th <150ms per token for mid-size models under provisioned load. We provide historical percentile charts and a fallback policy to ensure availability even when tail spikes happen — e.g., route to smaller model or a cached summary.

[06:16] Maya Chen: Quick interjection: customers often worry about cost when we suggest overprovisioning for Dedicated. That's where Redwood Optimize recommendations come in — it will suggest batching configs, quantization levels, and cache TTLs to save unit cost while hitting latency SLOs.

[06:34] Liam Torres: Can Optimize recommend model widths/quantization based on our real traffic?

[06:40] Maya Chen: Yes — we run a profiling pass on a sample workload and give a recommended configuration set: file-level estimates like expected tokens/unit cost, expected P95 latency, and an estimated monthly bill. We'll share an example spreadsheet.

[06:54] Alex Gomez: For POC we want to reproduce our workload — we can share traces. How invasive is the data collection?

[07:02] Ravi Patel: You can run a lightweight profiler that sends anonymized telemetry to Redwood, or for Private deployments we ship a profiling tool that runs in your VPC and writes results locally. No customer data leaves your env for Private mode. Hosted mode is tenant-isolated and we can sign a DPA.

[07:20] Priya Singh: Security: need SOC 2, SSO (SAML), audit logs, and KMS integration. Also data residency requirements for EU.

[07:28] Maya Chen: We have SOC 2 Type II, SAML/SCIM SSO support, and KMS integration for Private deployments — we'll attach the security pack. For EU residency we can route to region-specific infra or provide Private.

[07:40] Liam Torres: Does streaming telemetry contain PII? We want minimal exposure.

[07:45] Ravi Patel: Telemetry is metadata only unless you opt into sending payloads — we can redact/strip payloads at edge. We also support token-level redaction and retention policies.

[07:56] Alex Gomez: Back to timeouts — what are best practices for client-side SDKs to avoid partial outputs or duplication during reconnects?

[08:04] Ravi Patel: Use idempotency keys and resume tokens. We emit chunk sequence numbers and a resume cursor; SDK will attempt to resume from last acknowledged chunk. For duplicate chunks your client should dedupe by sequence.

[08:20] Liam Torres: If a model variant is unavailable mid-request and you fallback to another model, how do you ensure output consistency?

[08:28] Ravi Patel: Fallback might change output characteristics; we annotate responses with model metadata and a confidence tag. For strict consistency we recommend a canary window and gradual rollout; Redwood Console supports A/B/canary policies with automatic rollback if quality regressions detected by evals.

[08:46] Priya Singh: Can we see a quick demo of routing by token-length to a cheaper variant?

[08:50] [Ravi clicks around, editing a route policy]

[08:58] Ravi Patel: Here I set "If token_count > 32000 route->model-quantized-2x". Now I'll replay a request with 40k tokens.

[09:10] [replay run, console output shows route decision and model metadata]

[09:15] Alex Gomez: Metadata shows routed to quantized-2x and includes a note "fallback routed by token_length". Good. What's the performance delta?

[09:22] Ravi Patel: For this quantized variant we've seen ~2.2x throughput improvements and 30-40% cost reduction but higher hallucination risk in edge reasoning tasks — Optimize flags that tradeoff. You can also route only generation to quantized and keep retrieval/embedding on higher fidelity models.

[09:45] Liam Torres: We're concerned about hallucinations in safety-critical outputs. How do you handle quality monitoring?

[09:50] Maya Chen: Redwood Optimize includes evaluation runs and regression alerts tied to prompt sets. You can configure unit tests/prompts and get automatic quality regression notifications, and we keep traces to help debug.

[10:02] Alex Gomez: Is there an SDK instrumentation we should add?

[10:06] Ravi Patel: Minimal — the standard SDKs emit per-request metadata, token counts, error codes, and streaming chunk seq numbers. For deeper evals you can ship example prompts and references.

[10:18] Liam Torres: Ok this is helpful. Two more production questions: 1) network egress and regional compliance, 2) support for on-prem GPU with our KMS/HSM.

[10:28] Maya Chen: For egress/residency we can deploy in a region and provide Private with no egress if needed. For on-prem we've done air-gapped installs where KMS/HSM plugs in via customer network; Ravi can share the installation checklist.

[10:40] Ravi Patel: I'll attach the on-prem checklist and the KMS integration guide. It lists supported HSM vendors and steps.

[10:46] Priya Singh: For the POC we want a baseline test: 10k concurrent sessions with average 2k token context, and synthetic bursts to 1k TPS for 60s. Can Redwood run that or do we run locally?

[10:56] Ravi Patel: We can run it — two options: run a hosted benchmark in our infra with a signed test agreement, or we give you a runner and configs to run in your env. Hosted gives easier comparability; Private runs are more realistic for your network.

[11:10] Liam Torres: Costs?

[11:12] Maya Chen: We'll include estimates in the pricing doc — Optimize will also surface cost tradeoffs for the recommended config.

[11:18] Alex Gomez: One nit: logs in the Console sometimes use "K V cash" in transcriptions, just making sure docs are clear.

[11:24] Ravi Patel: Haha yeah that keeps happening in our transcripts; we standardized on "KV cache" in the docs.

[11:30] Maya Chen: We're about 45 minutes in — want to summarize and confirm next steps.

[11:36] Liam Torres: Sure. From Enso side: security pack, POC baseline test, and pricing. Priya will own SLO/latency details and confirm residency. Alex will share representative traces.

[11:46] Maya Chen: From Redwood: we'll send pricing and dedicated options, the streaming backpressure whitepaper, on-prem/KMS checklist, and run an initial baseline if you want hosted. We'll also schedule the POC scoping call.

[11:58] Priya Singh: One last question — do you have throttling limits per API key in hosted to protect us from noisy neighbors?

[12:04] Ravi Patel: Yes — per-key rate limiting, quotas, and route-level throttles. You can also set auto-burst rules and reserved throughput for critical routes.

[12:14] Liam Torres: OK thanks everyone, this was super helpful.

[12:18] Maya Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up with the materials.

[12:22] [meeting ends]

Notes on transcript: occasional transcription artifacts present (K V cash, T P S spelled out), some phrases run-on.
